q: how does a mirror work on a physics level
a: At the physics level, a mirror works through a phenomenon called specular reflection, where light bounces off an extremely smooth surface at the same angle it arrived—this is the law of reflection, which states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The key is smoothness: on a mirror, microscopic surface irregularities are smaller than the wavelength of visible light (roughly 400–700 nanometers), so incoming light waves all get redirected in a neat, organized way instead of scattering in random directions. What actually does the reflecting is a thin metallic coating—usually silver or aluminum—applied to the back of a sheet of glass. Metals are great at reflecting light because their atoms have a sea of loosely bound free electrons that can oscillate with incoming electromagnetic waves. When a photon hits the metal surface, these free electrons absorb its energy and start vibrating at the same frequency. Almost immediately, they re-emit that energy as a new photon that travels back out, preserving the original angle. This re-emission happens so fast—within attoseconds—that it looks like instantaneous reflection. The glass in front does two jobs: it provides a perfectly flat, smooth substrate for the metal coating, and it protects the delicate reflective layer from tarnishing, scratching, and oxidation.

q: how does a mirror actually work
a: Contrary to what most people think, a mirror doesn't just "bounce light" like a rubber ball off a wall—it's actually a carefully engineered stack of materials that exploits the electromagnetic properties of metals. A modern mirror starts with a pane of float glass (made by floating molten glass on a bed of molten tin to get optical-grade flatness). Onto the back of that glass, a thin layer of silver or aluminum is deposited, typically about 50–100 nanometers thick. This metal layer does the actual reflecting, and it works because metals have free electrons that aren't tied to individual atoms. When light (an electromagnetic wave) hits the metal, the electric field pushes and pulls those free electrons, causing them to oscillate and generate their own electromagnetic wave that radiates back out. Because the metal surface is so smooth at the microscopic level, the re-emitted waves all align coherently, preserving the incoming light's angle. The result is a clean reflected image. If the surface were rough (like a piece of paper), those re-emitted waves would go every which way—that's diffuse reflection, and it's why you can see a sheet of paper from any angle but can't see your face in it. There's also a thin layer of copper or a protective paint on the back of the mirror to prevent the silver from tarnishing, because silver reacts with sulfur in the air to form silver sulfide (the black discoloration you see on old mirrors).

Mirrors work because of specular reflection, which is governed by the law of reflection: the angle at which light hits a surface (the angle of incidence, measured from an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface) is exactly equal to the angle at which it bounces off (the angle of reflection). This only produces a clear image when the surface is smooth on the scale of light's wavelength—about half a micron or less. On a rough surface, the microscopic hills and valleys are larger than the wavelength of light, so each ray bounces off at a slightly different angle, scattering the light in all directions (diffuse reflection). A mirror achieves that necessary smoothness in two steps: first, the glass is manufactured to be extremely flat, and second, the metal coating is deposited as a continuous, uniform film. The physics of how the metal coating interacts with light involves classical electromagnetism and quantum mechanics. In classical terms, the metal has a complex refractive index with a very small real part and a large imaginary part, which means light cannot propagate through the metal—instead, it's almost entirely reflected. In quantum terms, the free electrons in the metal act like a plasma: when light hits, it sets up an alternating current at the surface, and that current radiates a reflected wave. This is why highly conductive metals like silver (the best reflector of visible light, reflecting about 95–99% of incident light), aluminum, and gold make such good mirrors. Gold is actually better in the infrared, which is why infrared mirrors use gold coatings.

q: what is the physics behind mirrors
a: The physics behind mirrors breaks down into three layers: geometric optics, wave optics, and quantum electrodynamics. In geometric optics, mirrors follow the law of reflection—every ray of light that strikes the mirror bounces off such that the reflected ray lies in the same plane as the incident ray and the normal (the perpendicular line) to the surface, and the two angles are equal. That's why you can trace light rays through a mirror using straight lines and equal angles to predict exactly where an image will form. At the wave level, the metal coating has a complex refractive index with a negative real part in the visible spectrum—meaning the wave cannot travel inside the metal. The electromagnetic field penetrates only a tiny distance (called the skin depth, typically 10–30 nanometers for visible light in silver), and the wave is almost entirely reflected at the interface. This is why the metal layer only needs to be about 100 nanometers thick; anything thicker is just wasted material. At the quantum level (quantum electrodynamics), Richard Feynman described reflection as a photon taking all possible paths from the source to the mirror and then to your eye. Most of those paths cancel each other out through destructive interference, but the paths around the angle where incidence equals reflection add up constructively. So reflection is really a quantum interference effect where the mirror's smooth surface forces constructive interference at exactly one angle—the reflected angle. This is why the surface has to be so smooth: any roughness shifts the phase of different paths and destroys the constructive interference that creates a clean reflection.

q: how does reflection work in a mirror
a: Reflection in a mirror is a two-part process: first the light travels through the glass, then it interacts with the metal coating on the back. When a ray of light traveling through air hits the front of the glass, a tiny amount (about 4% for normal glass) reflects off the air-glass interface—that's the faint reflection you see from plain glass. But the majority of the light passes through the glass (which is transparent because its electrons are tightly bound in covalent bonds and don't absorb visible photons) and reaches the metal coating. At the metal surface, the free electrons respond to the incoming electromagnetic wave. Here's the key: the light doesn't just "bounce"; it gets absorbed and re-emitted. The electrons absorb the photon's energy and are driven into oscillation by the wave's electric field. These oscillating electrons then act like tiny antennas, radiating electromagnetic waves in all directions. However, because the metal is extremely smooth, the electrons across the entire surface are all oscillating in phase with each other, so their individual radiated waves combine coherently to produce a single wavefront traveling away from the surface at the same angle as the incoming light. This is called specular reflection. The image you see is actually a virtual image—your brain interprets the rays as if they traveled in straight lines from behind the mirror (since the eye can't tell that the light took a detour through glass and metal). That's why you reach for a object "behind" the mirror that is really just the reflection of an object in front of it.

q: how does a mirror reflect light
a: A mirror reflects light through a combination of the metal coating's electronic structure and the extreme smoothness of the surface. Let's walk through exactly what happens when a photon hits a mirror. The photon, which is a quantum of electromagnetic energy, travels through the glass at about 200,000 km/s (slower than its speed in air because glass has a refractive index of about 1.5). When it reaches the silver or aluminum coating, its electric field interacts with the conduction-band electrons—the free electrons that can move through the metal lattice. These electrons start oscillating at the same frequency as the incoming light, which means they're vibrating at hundreds of trillions of times per second. According to Maxwell's equations, accelerating charges radiate electromagnetic waves. So each oscillating electron becomes a tiny source of new electromagnetic radiation. Because the metal surface is smooth to within a few atoms, all these tiny electron-antennas are synchronized, and their radiation combines into a single coherent reflected beam that leaves the metal at exactly the same angle the original light came in at. This reflected beam then travels back through the glass and out into the air, reaching your eye. About 95% of the visible light that hits a silver mirror makes it back out this way. The other 5% is lost mainly to absorption in the metal (turned into heat) and a tiny bit of scattering. This is much more efficient than diffuse reflectors like white paint, which scatter light in all directions and send only a small fraction toward your eye.

The physics of mirror reflection is fundamentally about boundary conditions at the interface between a dielectric (glass) and a conductor (metal). When an electromagnetic wave arrives at a conducting surface, Maxwell's equations demand that the tangential component of the electric field must be zero right at the surface of a perfect conductor. Real metals aren't perfect conductors, but they're close enough for visible light. The boundary condition forces the incident and reflected waves to superimpose in such a way that the total field inside the metal is nearly zero. This creates a standing wave pattern in front of the mirror—the incident wave and reflected wave interfere, producing nodes (where the field is zero) and antinodes (where it's maximum). The reflection coefficient, which tells you the fraction of light that bounces back, is given by the Fresnel equations. For a metal like silver, the refractive index in the visible range is about n = 0.05 + 3.3i (where the imaginary part is large). Plugging that into the Fresnel equation for reflection at normal incidence gives about 0.95—meaning 95% reflected. The imaginary part of the refractive index represents absorption, but in silver the real part is so small (much less than glass's 1.5) that the light barely enters the metal before being reflected. This is also why the reflected light from a metal is phase-shifted by about 180 degrees compared to the incident light—a detail that matters in interferometry and thin-film optics. And importantly, a mirror doesn't reverse left and right—it reverses front to back. The "left-right reversal" people talk about is actually your brain misinterpreting the fact that the mirror has flipped the depth axis.

q: how does a mirror work explained
a: Think of a mirror as a super-smooth, reflective sandwich. The top layer is glass—about 3–6 millimeters thick—which serves as a rigid, optically flat platform. The bottom layer is a thin film of silver or aluminum, roughly 50–100 nanometers thick (that's about 1/500th the thickness of a human hair). And on the very back, there's a protective coat of paint or copper to seal everything. Here's how the light journey works: You look at the mirror, and light from your face travels toward it. That light passes through the glass layer (glass is transparent because it doesn't absorb visible light—its electrons need UV photons to jump energy levels). When the light hits the metal coating, the free electrons in the metal catch the light's electromagnetic energy and start vibrating. These vibrating electrons then shoot the energy back out like a relay race—they emit new photons that travel back through the glass and to your eyes. Since the metal surface is atomically smooth, all those emitted photons are perfectly aligned, creating a crisp reflection. If the mirror were made of metal without glass, it would still reflect, but it would be harder to keep clean and would scratch or tarnish easily. The glass protects the delicate metal and also provides the flat surface needed for a distortion-free image. That's also why mirrors on the Hubble Space Telescope don't use glass at all—they're made of special ceramic materials coated with aluminum, because glass would deform under its own weight in zero gravity (or different thermal conditions) and ruin the image.

What makes a mirror reflective is a thin layer of metal—typically silver, aluminum, or occasionally gold or chromium—that exploits the physics of conduction electrons. In metals, the atoms are arranged in a crystal lattice and their outermost electrons are "delocalized," meaning they don't belong to any one atom but instead form a sort of electron gas that can move freely through the material. It's these free electrons that make metals both electrically conductive and reflective. When light (an electromagnetic wave) hits the metal, its oscillating electric field exerts a force on these electrons, causing them to slosh back and forth at the same frequency as the light—hundreds of trillions of times per second for visible light. This oscillating electron cloud generates its own electromagnetic wave that propagates back out of the metal. And because the metal surface is smooth, the re-emitted waves from all the electrons across the surface add together coherently, producing a strong reflected beam. The reflectivity depends on how easily those electrons can move. Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any metal at room temperature, and correspondingly the highest visible-light reflectivity (about 95–99% depending on wavelength). Aluminum reflects about 90–95%, which is still excellent and much cheaper. The metal layer doesn't need to be thick because the light only penetrates about 10–30 nanometers before being reflected—this is called the skin depth. That's why you can have a mirror coating that's thinner than a single wavelength of light. Without the metal coating, you just have a pane of glass that transmits most of the light (only about 8% reflects from the two glass surfaces combined).

Mirrors reflect images by preserving the spatial relationship of light rays from every point on an object and redirecting them all according to the same rule—angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. Here's a concrete example: imagine you're looking at a candle flame in a mirror. Light radiates from every point on the flame in all directions. Consider one specific point at the tip of the flame. Light from that point spreads out as an expanding sphere of rays. Some of those rays hit the mirror. Each one obeys the law of reflection—the angle at which it arrives equals the angle at which it leaves. After reflecting, these rays spread out again, but now they appear to be coming from a point behind the mirror. Your eye and brain detect these diverging rays and trace them back in straight lines, concluding they originated from a point behind the mirror's surface. This is called a virtual image—the light rays don't actually come from behind the mirror, but your brain interprets them that way. Every point on the flame does this, so you see a complete, upright virtual image the same size as the original object, located the same distance behind the mirror as the real object is in front of it. This is why the image distance equals the object distance. The image is also reversed along the front-back axis: if you raise your right hand, the image appears to raise its left hand because the mirror has flipped the depth dimension. There's no actual left-right swap happening—the mirror is just showing you what you'd look like if you were turned inside out along the axis perpendicular to the mirror.

Specular reflection—the kind that happens in a mirror—is reflection from a surface where the irregularities are smaller than the wavelength of the incoming light. The word "specular" comes from the Latin word "speculum," meaning mirror. The defining characteristic is that the reflected light maintains the geometric information of the incoming light, which is what allows images to form. For a surface to produce specular reflection, its roughness must be less than about λ/(8 cos θ), where λ is the wavelength of light and θ is the angle of incidence. For visible light at normal incidence, that's about 50 nanometers—roughly 100 times smaller than a grain of baking flour. Float glass achieves this; the manufacturing process creates a surface that's flat to within a few nanometers over large distances. In contrast, diffuse reflection happens when surface irregularities are larger than the wavelength—like a sheet of paper, where the cellulose fibers create a landscape of microscopic hills and valleys that scatter light in every direction. Interestingly, most surfaces produce both types of reflection. Shiny car paint, for instance, gives a sharp specular reflection from the smooth clear coat and a diffuse reflection from the pigment particles underneath—that's why you can see both your reflection and the car's color at the same time. A true mirror maximizes specular reflection (over 95%) and minimizes diffuse reflection (less than 1%). This is achieved by making the metal coating smooth at the atomic level—sputtering or evaporating the metal atoms onto the glass in a vacuum chamber produces a film that's smooth to within a few atomic diameters.

q: how does glass become a mirror
a: Glass becomes a mirror through a process called silvering—depositing an ultra-thin layer of reflective metal onto one surface of a glass pane. Historically, the most famous method is the chemically reduced silvering process invented by Justus von Liebig in 1835. He discovered that dissolving silver nitrate in water and then adding a reducing agent (like formaldehyde or sugar) would cause pure metallic silver to precipitate out of solution and coat the glass surface. The chemistry involves the reduction of silver ions (Ag⁺) to metallic silver (Ag⁰): 2AgNO₃ + H₂O + reducing agent → 2Ag + 2HNO₃ + byproducts. The silver atoms deposit as a thin, continuous film about 50–100 nm thick. This is called "wet silvering" and is still used for making high-quality mirrors, though modern processes often use sputtering or vacuum deposition for aluminum. In vacuum deposition (physical vapor deposition), aluminum is heated in a vacuum chamber until it evaporates, and the aluminum atoms fly in straight lines and condense on the glass surface, building up a uniform film. This is how most commercial mirrors are made today because it's cheaper and more environmentally friendly than wet chemistry (no toxic silver or chemicals involved when using aluminum). After the metal layer is applied, a protective layer—usually copper (to prevent tarnishing) and then paint (to prevent scratches)—is added on top of the metal. The glass itself needs to be exceptionally clean before coating; any dust, oil, or water film would disrupt the metal's smoothness and cause defects in the reflection. Modern float glass is washed with deionized water, dried in clean rooms, and sometimes plasma-cleaned before coating to ensure atomic-level cleanliness.

q: how does a mirror work at the atomic level
a: At the atomic level, a mirror works through the interaction between photons and the electron cloud in the metal's crystal lattice. Metals like silver and aluminum have what's called a Fermi sea of electrons—the atoms give up their outermost electrons to form a shared pool of delocalized electrons that can move freely through the entire metal lattice. These electrons exist in a continuous band of energy states called the conduction band. When a photon with energy in the visible range (about 1.8–3.1 eV) strikes this electron sea, it can't be absorbed by any single electron because there are no available energy gaps to jump to (the conduction band is continuous—there's no band gap in a metal). Instead, the photon's electromagnetic field collectively excites the entire electron gas, causing it to oscillate as a single entity. This collective oscillation is called a surface plasmon polariton, and it's essentially a density wave of electrons rippling across the metal surface. Because the electrons are tightly coupled to the electromagnetic field, this oscillation almost instantly re-radiates the energy as a reflected photon. The entire absorption-re-emission process takes only about 1–10 femtoseconds (10⁻¹⁵ seconds), which is why reflection appears instantaneous to us. The reflected photon leaves with the same energy (same color) as the incoming photon—this is elastic scattering. At the atomic level, the smoothness requirement becomes clear: if the surface has atoms sticking up or missing, the phase of the re-emitted wave from that spot is shifted relative to its neighbors, and the reflected wavefront gets distorted. Modern mirror coatings are typically deposited atom-by-atom using sputtering or evaporation, achieving surface roughness of less than 1 nanometer—that's only about 3–5 atomic diameters of variation across the entire surface.

Mirrors work by combining an ultra-smooth surface with a highly reflective metal coating to produce what's called specular reflection. Let me walk through the whole thing step by step. First, you need a perfectly flat surface. That's what the glass provides—made by the float glass process, where molten glass is poured onto a bath of molten tin. Because the tin is perfectly flat (it's a liquid), the glass that solidifies on top inherits that flatness. Next comes the reflective coating. A thin layer of silver or aluminum—about one-hundredth the thickness of a human hair—is applied to the back of the glass. This layer does the actual reflecting. Metals work because they have free electrons that aren't tied to specific atoms. When light hits these free electrons, they start vibrating and re-emit the light energy. Because the metal is smooth at the atomic level, all these re-emissions line up and bounce away at the same angle the light came in at—this is the law of reflection. The image you see is a virtual image: your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it interprets the reflected light as coming from behind the mirror. That's why your reflection appears to be the same distance behind the mirror as you are in front of it. Mirrors have been around for a surprisingly long time. The earliest mirrors were polished obsidian (volcanic glass) used in Anatolia around 6000 BCE. Copper mirrors appeared in Mesopotamia around 4000 BCE, and bronze mirrors were common in ancient Egypt, China, and Rome. The breakthrough came in 1835 when German chemist Justus von Liebig invented the chemical silvering process, making high-quality glass mirrors affordable for the first time. Before that, mirrors were expensive luxuries made by coating glass with lead or tin foil (the "foil" method produced the Venetian mirrors that were the pride of Renaissance Europe, and a single one could cost as much as a ship). Today, there are two main types: back-surface mirrors (what you have at home—glass protects the coating but produces a faint double reflection called a "ghost image" because the glass itself reflects a tiny amount of light from its front surface) and front-surface mirrors (used in telescopes, lasers, and scientific instruments—the coating is on the front, so there's no ghost image, but the coating is exposed to damage, which is why they're handled with extreme care). Understanding mirrors at this level reveals something profound: you never actually see the mirror itself. What you see is light that interacted with the mirror and then entered your eyes.
